implementation_notes: Python ships the pattern in the standard library for threads: threading.Semaphore(value) blocks in acquire() and returns a permit in release(n), and both it and BoundedSemaphore support the context-manager protocol, so 'with slots:' is the release-on-every-exit-path form. BoundedSemaphore additionally raises ValueError when release() would exceed the initial value - the cheap over-release guard that plain Semaphore lacks, and the reason the docs recommend it whenever the resource size is fixed. The hand-written condition-variable version is never needed.
pitfalls: threading.Semaphore has no upper bound: an extra release() silently raises the counter, so prefer BoundedSemaphore whenever the capacity is fixed.
Python's acquire() may be interrupted by signals in the main thread and raises KeyboardInterrupt out of the wait; a permit is not held when that happens, but cleanup must not release blindly.
A semaphore is not reentrant: a thread that acquires twice without releasing deadlocks against itself once the bound is reached.

variants.name: asyncio.Semaphore / asyncio.BoundedSemaphore
variants.idiom_name: asyncio.Semaphore(value) with async acquire and async with
variants.implementation_notes: For asyncio tasks, asyncio.Semaphore(value) provides the same counter with an awaitable acquire() and the 'async with sem:' release-on-exit form; the primitive is not thread-safe and never blocks the event loop, which is exactly why it must be used instead of threading.Semaphore inside coroutines. asyncio.BoundedSemaphore raises ValueError on over-release just like its threading counterpart. Use the threading primitive across OS threads and the asyncio one within a single event loop; sharing either across that boundary is a bug.
variants.code_sketch:
slots = asyncio.Semaphore(8)

async def handle(req):
    async with slots:                   # suspends, never blocks the loop
        return await serve(req)
pitfalls: asyncio primitives are not thread-safe; calling acquire() from another thread corrupts the loop's internal state - use asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe or a threading primitive instead.
Blocking on threading.Semaphore inside a coroutine stalls the entire event loop, defeating the purpose of the async semaphore.
asyncio.Semaphore has no fairness guarantee across tasks in all versions and no timeout argument; wrap acquisition in asyncio.wait_for when a deadline is required.
